senses.definition: (informal) Very minor damage caused by being struck; a small dent or chip.
examples: If you surf regularly, then you're going to ding your board. Here's a rough guide on how to repair them... If the ding is on the rail, run tape across the ding conforming to the rail curve, leaving a gap to pour in resin and make sure it is sealed to prevent resin escaping and forming dribbles.

quotes.text: Mike hit the bottom and picked up a little ding on his head.
quotes.reference: 1966, Bruce Brown, director, The Endless Summer:

examples: I just got my first ding letter.

quotes.text: to ding the book a coit's distance from him
quotes.reference: 1644, John Milton, Areopagitica; a Speech of Mr. John Milton for the Liberty of Unlicenc’d Printing, to the Parlament of England, London: [s.n.], →OCLC:

quotes.text: The butcher's axe (like great Alcides' bat) / Dings deadly downe ten thousand thousand flat.

senses.definition: (transitive) To inflict minor damage upon, especially by hitting or striking.
examples: If you surf regularly, then you're going to ding your board.
His top school dinged him last week.

senses.definition: (transitive, colloquial) To deduct, as points, from (somebody), in the manner of a penalty; to penalize.
examples: My bank dinged me three bucks for using their competitor's ATM.

quotes.text: […] [E]mployees don't feel like they're going to get dinged on performance reviews because they had the same goals as a guy who had been there all 12 months with no leave.
quotes.reference: 2015 August 7, Ron Lieber, “Bringing paternity leave into the mainstream [print version: Paid leave expands for fathers, but will there be any takers?, International New York Times, 10 August 2015, p. 14]”, in The New York Times:

senses.definition: (Scotland, of rain) To fall heavily and continually, with great force.

quotes.text: The night turn'd dark an' dang on rain, […]
quotes.reference: 1821, William Liddle (of Edinburgh.), Poems on different occasions, chiefly in the Scottish dialect, page 226:

quotes.text: An awfu' show'r o' sna' and drift / As ever dang down frae the lift; / Right wild an' monstrous Boreas roar'd.
quotes.reference: 1832, John Burness, Thrummy Cap, a Tale [in Verse]; and The Brownie O' Fearnden, a Ballad, page 4:

senses.definition: The high-pitched resonant sound of a bell.
(colloquial, roleplaying games, especially video games) The act of levelling up.
(intransitive) To make a high-pitched resonant sound like a bell.

quotes.text: The fretful tinkling of the convent bell evermore dinging among the mountain echoes.
quotes.reference: 1824, Geoffrey Crayon [pseudonym; Washington Irving], Tales of a Traveller, (please specify |part=1 to 4), Philadelphia, Pa.: H[enry] C[harles] Carey & I[saac] Lea, […], →OCLC:

quotes.text: These were succeeded by anchor and chain-cable forges, where sledgehammers were dinging upon iron all day long.
quotes.reference: 1846 October 1 – 1848 April 1, Charles Dickens, Dombey and Son, London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1848, →OCLC:

senses.definition: (transitive) To keep repeating; impress by reiteration, with reference to the monotonous striking of a bell.

quotes.text: If I'm to have any good, let it come of itself; not keep dinging it, dinging it into one so.

senses.definition: (intransitive, colloquial, roleplaying games, especially video games) To level up.
